x.ASV: A Psalm of David. Jehovah is my light and my salvation; Whom shall I fear? Jehovah is the strength of my life; Of whom shall I be afraid?
x.Darby: [A Psalm] of David. Jehovah is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? Jehovah is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
x.KJV: A Psalm of David. The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
x.YLT: By David. Jehovah is my light and my salvation, Whom do I fear? Jehovah is the strength of my life, Of whom am I afraid?

nt: David is speaking of **Yahweh** as if he were **light** that illuminates, guides, helps, and encourages him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is like light to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the one who saves me]

David is using two rhetorical questions, **whom will I fear** and **whom will I dread**, to emphasize that he does not fear anyone because Yahweh protects him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements. Alternate translation: [there is no one I fear … there is no one I dread] or [there is no one I need to fear … there is no one I need to dread]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a physical location, a **refuge**, that could provide safety and protection. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Yahweh protects my life like a place of refuge] or [Yahweh is like a safe place for me where I can go to be safe]

x.ASV: When evil-doers came upon me to eat up my flesh, Even mine adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell.
x.Darby: When evil-doers, mine adversaries and mine enemies, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell.
x.KJV: When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell.
x.YLT: When evil doers come near to me to eat my flesh, My adversaries and mine enemies to me, They have stumbled and fallen.

nt: David is speaking of his enemies’ attacks as if they were wild animals trying **to devour** his **flesh**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly or express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [to destroy me completely] or [to attack me like wild beasts]

The terms **enemies** and **the ones being hostile to me** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my fierce enemies]

Here, **they stumbled and fell** represents being defeated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were defeated] or [they failed in their attack]

x.ASV: Though a host should encamp against me, My heart shall not fear: Though war should rise against me, Even then will I be confident.
x.Darby: If a host encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; if war rise against me, in this will I be confident.
x.KJV: Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident.
x.YLT: Though a host doth encamp against me, My heart doth not fear, Though war riseth up against me, In this I am confident.

nt: אִם־תַּחֲנֶ֬ה עָלַ֨⁠י ׀ מַחֲנֶה֮ לֹֽא־יִירָ֪א לִ֫בִּ֥⁠י אִם־תָּק֣וּם עָ֭לַ⁠י מִלְחָמָ֑ה בְּ֝⁠זֹ֗את אֲנִ֣י בוֹטֵֽחַ

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Though an army encamps against me and war arises against me, my heart will not fear but will be confident]

In this verse, the word **army** is singular in form, but it refers to all soldiers as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning of “army” in another way. Alternate translation: [Though enemy troops encamp against me]

Here David is speaking of **my heart** as if it were the part of him that experiences fear. In your language, it may be more natural to say that David himself will not fear. Alternate translation: [I will not fear]

David is using **war arises against me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “when enemies attack me” or “when I am attacked in battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [though enemies attack me] or [though I am under attack]

x.ASV: One thing have I asked of Jehovah, that will I seek after: That I may dwell in the house of Jehovah all the days of my life, To behold the beauty of Jehovah, And to inquire in his temple.
x.Darby: One [thing] have I asked of Jehovah, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of Jehovah all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of Jehovah, and to inquire [of him] in his temple.
x.KJV: One thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the Lord, and to enquire in his temple.
x.YLT: One thing I asked of Jehovah--it I seek. My dwelling in the house of Jehovah, All the days of my life, To look on the pleasantness of Jehovah, And to inquire in His temple.

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [One thing I have asked from Yahweh, yes, this is what I will seek]

Here David is speaking of the object of his desire (dwelling in God’s tabernacle) as if it were something he could physically pursue or chase after. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I long for] or [that I desire]
See how you translated the similar phrase “and I will dwell in the house of Yahweh for length of days” in [23:6](../023/006.md).

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were actually looking at the physical **beauty** of Yahweh with his eyes. He means that he wants to experience and appreciate Yahweh’s wonderful character and presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to experience Yahweh’s wonderful presence] or [to appreciate Yahweh’s glorious character]

David is speaking of the **temple** of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in his tabernacle]

x.ASV: For in the day of trouble he will keep me secretly in his pavilion: In the covert of his tabernacle will he hide me; He will lift me up upon a rock.
x.Darby: For in the day of evil he will hide me in his pavilion; in the secret of his tent will he keep me concealed: he will set me high upon a rock.
x.KJV: For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock.
x.YLT: For He hideth me in a tabernacle in the day of evil, He hideth me in a secret place of His tent, On a rock he raiseth me up.

nt: כִּ֤י יִצְפְּנֵ֨⁠נִי ׀ בְּ⁠סֻכֹּ⁠ה֮ בְּ⁠י֪וֹם רָ֫עָ֥ה יַ֭סְתִּרֵ⁠נִי בְּ⁠סֵ֣תֶר אָהֳל֑⁠וֹ

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [For in the day of trouble he will hide me in his hut, yes, he will conceal me in his tent]

David assumes that readers will know that **his hut** and **his tent** refer to God’s tabernacle. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he will hide me in his tabernacle; he will hide me in the hiding-place of his sacred tent] or [he will hide me in his tabernacle; he will hide me in the hiding-place of his tabernacle]

Here David is referring to Yahweh’s tabernacle as a **hut** and **tent** and is speaking as if Yahweh was actually hiding him from his enemies there. David means that by his being in Yahweh’s tabernacle, Yahweh will protect him from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will protect me and keep me safe in his tabernacle]

David is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time of distress or difficulty. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I have trouble] or [in times of trouble]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I am troubled]

David is speaking of Yahweh protecting him and keeping him safe as if Yahweh would literally lift him up and place him on a high **rock** where he would be safe from the attacks of his enemies. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison as in the UST.

x.ASV: And now shall my head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me; And I will offer in his tabernacle sacrifices of joy; I will sing, yea, I will sing praises unto Jehovah.
x.Darby: And now shall my head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me; and I will offer in his tent sacrifices of shouts of joy: I will sing, yea, I will sing psalms unto Jehovah.
x.KJV: And now shall mine head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me: therefore will I offer in his tabernacle sacrifices of joy; I will sing, yea, I will sing praises unto the Lord.
x.YLT: And now, lifted up is my head, Above my enemies--my surrounders, And I sacrifice in His tent sacrifices of shouting, I sing, yea, I sing praise to Jehovah.

nt: David is using **my head will be lifted up** as a common expression of his culture to mean “I will be exalted” or “I will triumph.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And now I will be exalted above]
See how you translated the phrase “his tent” in the previous verse where it is used with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [in his tabernacle]

By **sacrifices of a shout of joy**, David means sacrifices that he offers while shouting joyfully to God. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will joyfully shout as I sacrifice in his tent]

x.ASV: Hear, O Jehovah, when I cry with my voice: Have mercy also upon me, and answer me.
x.Darby: Hear, Jehovah; with my voice do I call; be gracious unto me, and answer me.
x.KJV: Hear, O Lord, when I cry with my voice: have mercy also upon me, and answer me.
x.YLT: Hear, O Jehovah, my voice--I call, And favour me, and answer me.

nt: Here David is using the imperative forms **Hear**, **be gracious to me**, and **answer me**, but he intends to communicate polite requests rather than commands. If these imperative forms do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear, Yahweh, my voice when I cry out, and please be gracious to me, and answer me]

Here, **voice** represents David’s prayer or request. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my request when I cry out]

x.ASV: When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, Jehovah, will I seek.
x.Darby: My heart said for thee, Seek ye my face. Thy face, O Jehovah, will I seek.
x.KJV: When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, Lord, will I seek.
x.YLT: To Thee said my heart `They sought my face, Thy face, O Jehovah, I seek.'

nt: לְ⁠ךָ֤ ׀ אָמַ֣ר לִ֭בִּ⁠י בַּקְּשׁ֣וּ פָנָ֑⁠י אֶת־פָּנֶ֖י⁠ךָ יְהוָ֣ה אֲבַקֵּֽשׁ

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [When you said, “Seek my face,” my heart said to you, “Your face, Yahweh, I will seek.”]

The Hebrew verb the ULT translates as **Seek** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing his people or people in general who are willing to seek and trust him, and not just David. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and desires exist. David is speaking of his inner self as if it were his physical heart that could speak. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My inner self] or [I]

Here, **face** represents being in the presence of God and also God’s favor and intervention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my presence and help … Your presence and help]

x.ASV: Hide not thy face from me; Put not thy servant away in anger: Thou hast been my help; Cast me not off, neither forsake me, O God of my salvation.
x.Darby: Hide not thy face from me; put not thy servant away in anger: thou hast been my help; cast me not off, neither forsake me, OGod of my salvation.
x.KJV: Hide not thy face far from me; put not thy servant away in anger: thou hast been my help; leave me not, neither forsake me, O God of my salvation.
x.YLT: Hide not Thy face from me, Turn not aside in anger Thy servant, My help Thou hast been. Leave me not, nor forsake me, O God of my salvation.

nt: These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not hide your face from me; please do not turn your servant away in anger … Please do not abandon me or leave me]

David is using **hide your face** as a common expression of his culture to mean “reject me” or “turn away from me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not reject me] or [Do not turn away from me]

The terms **abandon** and **leave** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Do not forsake me]
See how you translated the phrase “God of my salvation” in [18:46](../018/046.md) where it occurs with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [the God who saves me]

x.ASV: When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.
x.Darby: For had my father and my mother forsaken me, then had Jehovah taken me up.
x.KJV: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me up.
x.YLT: When my father and my mother Have forsaken me, then doth Jehovah gather me.

nt: Because David does not explain in what way his father and mother have left him, it is best not to add any additional explanatory information to your translation to clarify how or why his parents might have left him. It is suggested that you simply translate this phrase as it is. It may be that David’s father and mother had died by this time in his life and had not intentionally left him.

x.ASV: Teach me thy way, O Jehovah; And lead me in a plain path, Because of mine enemies.
x.Darby: Teach me thy way, Jehovah, and lead me in an even path, because of mine enemies.
x.KJV: Teach me thy way, O Lord, and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies.
x.YLT: Shew me, O Jehovah, Thy way, And lead me in a path of uprightness, For the sake of my beholders.

nt: ה֤וֹרֵ֥⁠נִי יְהוָ֗ה דַּ֫רְכֶּ֥⁠ךָ וּ֭⁠נְחֵ⁠נִי בְּ⁠אֹ֣רַח מִישׁ֑וֹר

Here David uses imperative forms, but he is making polite requests rather than giving commands. If the imperative form does not communicate a polite request in your language, then use a form that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please teach me your way, Yahweh, and please lead me on a level path]
See how you translated the similar phrase “make me know your ways” in [25:4](../025/004.md).

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh would **lead** him **on a level path**. He is picturing his life as if it were a journey and asking Yahweh to guide him along a smooth, safe route. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

David is using **because of my enemies** to give the reason for the result that **lead me on a level path** describes. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because of my enemies, lead me on a level path]

x.ASV: Deliver me not over unto the will of mine adversaries: For false witnesses are risen up against me, And such as breathe out cruelty.
x.Darby: Deliver me not over to the will of mine adversaries; for false witnesses are risen up against me, and such as breathe out violence.
x.KJV: Deliver me not over unto the will of mine enemies: for false witnesses are risen up against me, and such as breathe out cruelty.
x.YLT: Give me not to the will of my adversaries, For risen against me have false witnesses, And they breathe out violence to me.

nt: אַֽל־תִּ֭תְּנֵ⁠נִי בְּ⁠נֶ֣פֶשׁ צָרָ֑⁠י כִּ֥י קָֽמוּ־בִ֥⁠י עֵֽדֵי־שֶׁ֝֗קֶר וִ⁠יפֵ֥חַ חָמָֽס

David is giving the reason why God should not give him up to his enemies. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second and third phrases give the reasons for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because false witnesses have risen against me, and a witness of violence, do not give me up to the desire of my adversaries]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. David is asking God not to hand him over to his enemies. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not give me up]

David is using **give me up to the desire of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “deliver me over to” or “hand me over to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not deliver me over to the desire of my adversaries]

David assumes that readers will know that **the desire of my adversaries** refers to the harmful things that his enemies want to do to him. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Do not deliver me over to my adversaries so that they can do the harmful things they desire to do to me]

David is using **have risen against me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “have taken action to oppose me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have opposed me]

The Hebrew word that the ULT translates as **a witness of** could be either: (1) a noun that means “a testifier” or “a witness.” Alternate translation: [and a testifier of violence] or [and a violent testifier who is violent] or (2) an adjective that means “one breathing out” or “one puffing out.” Alternate translation: [and one who breathes out violence]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **witness** that is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a violent witness] or [and a witness who speaks violently]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a witness who plans violent things] or [and a witness who acts violently]

x.ASV: I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of Jehovah In the land of the living.
x.Darby: Unless I had believed to see the goodness of Jehovah in the land of the living...!
x.KJV: I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.
x.YLT: I had not believed to look on the goodness of Jehovah In the land of the living!

nt: לׅׄוּלֵׅׄ֗אׅׄ הֶ֭אֱמַנְתִּי לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת בְּֽ⁠טוּב־יְהוָ֗ה בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ חַיִּֽים

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Unless I had believed that I would look on the goodness of Yahweh in the land of the living, I would have grown discouraged] or [I am certain that I will see the goodness of Yahweh in the land of the living]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Unless I had believed that I would see Yahweh do good things for me]

David is using **in the land of the living** as a common expression of his culture to mean “while I am still alive” or “during my lifetime.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while I am still alive] or [during my lifetime]

x.ASV: Wait for Jehovah: Be strong, and let thy heart take courage; Yea, wait thou for Jehovah.
x.Darby: Wait for Jehovah; be strong and let thy heart take courage: yea, wait for Jehovah.
x.KJV: Wait on the Lord: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the Lord.
x.YLT: Look unto Jehovah--be strong, And He doth strengthen thy heart, Yea, look unto Jehovah!

nt: See how you translated the similar expressions in [25:3](../025/003.md), [25:5](../025/005.md), and [25:21](../025/021.md).
קַוֵּ֗ה אֶל־יְה֫וָ֥ה חֲ֭זַק וְ⁠יַאֲמֵ֣ץ לִבֶּ֑⁠ךָ וְ֝⁠קַוֵּ֗ה אֶל־יְהוָֽה

The words that the ULT translates as **wait**, **your**, and **be courageous** are all singular here. David is either speaking to himself or to some other individual, or he is speaking collectively to each individual person experiencing discouragement or fear who might hear or read this psalm. So use the singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The terms **Be strong** and **let your heart be courageous** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Be very courageous]

Here David is speaking of **heart** as if it were something that could be courageous. The heart represents a person’s inner being or emotions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and be courageous within yourself] or [and be inwardly courageous]
